---
title: "Quiz: colocalisation"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A merged green/magenta image shows many white spots. Why is that not enough to claim colocalisation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What decides how bright each channel looks in the merge?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The colour depends on the display range chosen for each channel, on bleed-through, on misalignment and on resolution: spots can look white because one channel leaks into the other, or because two separate structures lie within one blurred spot. A claim needs coefficients over a defined region, thresholds, and controls.
:::

---

**Q2.** Two channels are imaged with different gains and offsets on two days. Which of Pearson's $r$ and the overlap coefficient can be compared between the days?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which one subtracts the means?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Pearson's $r$: it subtracts the means and divides by the spreads, so offsets and (positive) gains cancel. The overlap coefficient uses the raw values, so a different offset changes it.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does including the dark background around cells raise Pearson's $r$, even for independent structures?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Draw the scatter plot with two clusters.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The background pixels form a cluster that is dark in both channels; the cell pixels form one that is brighter in both (diffuse signal, autofluorescence). A line through the two clusters explains much of the variance, so $r$ is high. It measures "both channels are in the cells", not "the structures overlap". Measure inside the cells.
:::

---

**Q4.** Small vesicles of protein A all lie inside large compartments of protein B, which also contain much else. What do you expect for M1 and M2?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
M1: how much of A is where B is.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
M1 close to 1 (all of A is inside B), M2 small (most of B has no A). Pearson's $r$ would be moderate and hide the asymmetry (demo: M1 = 0.79, M2 = 0.32, $r$ = 0.37).
:::

---

**Q5.** Someone reports M1 = 0.98 and M2 = 0.97 for two unrelated proteins. What is the most likely mistake?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is "above threshold" when the threshold is 0?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No (or too low) thresholds: with a background offset and noise, every pixel is above 0 in both channels, so all of A is "where B is" and vice versa. Thresholds above the background (for example Costes') are essential.
:::

---

**Q6.** The randomisation test gives $p < 0.02$ (none of 50 block-shuffled images reaches the observed $r$). Does that prove that the two proteins colocalise?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What would bleed-through do to the observed and the shuffled $r$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. It shows that the overlap in these two images is more than chance. Bleed-through, chromatic misalignment that happens to fit, or structures below the resolution limit all produce real overlap in the images without the proteins being together. The test cannot replace compensation, registration and biological controls.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why does shifting one channel by 2–3 pixels make $r$ drop sharply for small spots but hardly for large structures?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the shift with the size of the structures.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
After the shift, a spot of radius 2 px no longer overlaps its partner; a structure of radius 20 px still overlaps it almost entirely. $r$ falls off over about the size of the structures (the autocorrelation width). This is also why chromatic misalignment matters most for small structures.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* For channels with $B = aA + c + \varepsilon$ (noise $\varepsilon$ independent of $A$, variance $\sigma^2$), express $r$ in terms of $a$, $\operatorname{var} A$ and $\sigma^2$. What happens when the noise grows?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\operatorname{cov}(A, B) = a \operatorname{var} A$, $\operatorname{var} B = a^2 \operatorname{var} A + \sigma^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$r = \dfrac{a\operatorname{var}A}{\sqrt{\operatorname{var}A\,(a^2\operatorname{var}A + \sigma^2)}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \sigma^2/(a^2 \operatorname{var} A)}}$ (for $a > 0$). It falls towards 0 as the noise grows, although the colocalisation is perfect: $r$ mixes colocalisation with signal-to-noise ratio. (Demo: 0.99 at noise σ = 4, 0.88 at σ = 15.)
:::
